body.text: The prescribed proxy amount (PPA) is a notional amount, fixed at 55% of the SR&ED salary base under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, that Canadian claimants electing the proxy method add on Line 502 of Form T661 in lieu of actual overhead. It increases qualified expenditures for the investment tax credit but never enters the Section 37 pool.

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is the federal government's foundational fiscal mechanism for stimulating private-sector research, experimental engineering, and technological innovation, delivering $4.2 billion annually in tax support. Across the country, approximately 16,000 to over 19,000 corporate T2 claims and roughly 4,500 individual T1 claims are filed annually. Governed jointly by the Department of Finance Canada—which formulates statutory tax policy—and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)—which administers technical eligibility reviews and financial audits—the program operates through a dual-pillar statutory architecture under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945. The first pillar, codified in Section 37 of the ITA, allows taxpayers to pool and deduct allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures against business income in the current taxation year or carry them forward indefinitely. The second pillar, codified in Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA, provides an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Following the enactment of the Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1 (Bill C-15, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the Canadian SR&ED regime has undergone its most substantial structural expansion in over a decade. Effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), the federal government doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million, broadened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective three-year average revenue phase-out alternative for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), and extended the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). Concurrently, Bill C-15 reinstated the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures (depreciable property), equipment lease outlays, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024, while the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, providing up-front technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks. At the provincial level, Quebec fundamentally restructured its innovation landscape for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing eight legacy tax measures and replacing them with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) at rates of 30% on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% on excess spending.

Claimants navigating this modernized landscape must adhere to strict statutory deadlines and evidentiary standards. Under subsections 37(11), 37(12), and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, prescribed forms—specifically Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals))—must be filed within 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date (18 months after taxation year-end for corporations). Courts have consistently affirmed that this 18-month reporting deadline operates as a strict statutory bar without ministerial discretion for late-filing relief. Furthermore, while the CRA updated its administrative guidance in August 2021 into the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives—framing eligibility around the two core requirements of "Why" (scientific or technological advancement to resolve uncertainty) and "How" (systematic investigation or search)—the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72) that the five-criteria common-law framework established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) remains the authoritative legal standard for statutory eligibility.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The legal foundation for all federal R&D tax incentives in Canada rests on the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Unlike financial accounting standards or general commercial terminology, what is colloquially understood in industry as "research and development" (R&D) does not automatically constitute SR&ED for Canadian income tax purposes. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and structures the scope of qualifying and non-qualifying activities into three primary categories of core work (paragraphs (a) through (c)), one category of derivative support work (paragraph (d)), and seven explicit statutory exclusions (paragraphs (e) through (k)).
Under paragraphs 248(1)(a) through (c), core eligible SR&ED comprises three distinct categories of scientific or technological endeavour:

items: Basic Research (Paragraph 248(1)(a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research is typically conducted in laboratory or academic environments—frequently involving third-party payments to universities, research institutes, or scientific consortia—where hypotheses in theoretical or natural sciences (such as elementary particle physics, chemistry, or biology) are formulated and tested by experiment or analysis to discover new scientific principles or properties.

Applied Research (Paragraph 248(1)(b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. While sharing the requirement to generate new scientific knowledge through systematic investigation, applied research directs that inquiry toward solving a defined operational, clinical, or industrial problem.

Experimental Development (Paragraph 248(1)(c)): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada. Crucially, the statutory inclusion of "incremental improvements" confirms that a radical breakthrough or entirely novel invention is not required; rather, step-by-step advancements in underlying technological capability or engineering knowledge qualify, provided the work seeks to overcome a genuine technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved through standard practice or publicly available engineering knowledge.

body.text: Paragraph 248(1)(d) extends the definition of SR&ED to encompass support work, defined as work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but strictly to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work does not constitute SR&ED on its own. If a taxpayer or an arm's-length contractor performs computer programming, engineering design, or physical testing without a direct nexus to an underlying Canadian basic research, applied research, or experimental development project, the activity fails paragraph 248(1)(d). Furthermore, the "commensurate with the needs" threshold limits eligible support work to the exact volume, duration, and scope necessary to execute the experiments or analyses aimed at resolving the scientific or technological uncertainty.

Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) codify seven explicit statutory exclusions. Work with respect to any of the following activities is excluded from the definition of SR&ED, even if it occurs within the broader lifecycle of an innovative commercial project:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion (including consumer surveys, market validation, and promotional demonstrations supplementing advertising or selling).

Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes (such as standard quality assurance verification, compliance testing against known specifications, or routine debugging).
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities.
Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas.
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes (such as cosmetic alterations, aesthetic redesigns, or user-interface re-skinning lacking underlying technological uncertainty).
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection (gathering data using standard instruments or methods without supporting an active experimental hypothesis).

body.text: 1.2 The Dual-Pillar Statutory Mechanism: Section 37 and Sections 127 / 127.1

Calculating a federal SR&ED claim requires executing two legally related but mechanically distinct statutory computations: first, determining the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under Section 37 of the ITA; and second, determining qualified expenditures for the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA. Tax practitioners and auditors must never treat "allowable SR&ED expenditure" (Section 37) and "qualified SR&ED expenditure" (Section 127) as interchangeable terms, as an expenditure can be 100% deductible under Section 37 while generating a reduced ITC, a deferred ITC, or no ITC at all under Section 127.

body.text: Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct an amount not exceeding the positive balance in its pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures at the end of the taxation year. Because the Section 37 pool operates as a cumulative running balance, any undeducted portion does not expire and may be carried forward indefinitely to shelter business income in future taxation years (subject to loss restriction event rules under subsection 37(6.1)). However, if an SR&ED investment tax credit is claimed in a given year—whether applied to reduce Part I tax payable, carried back to a prior year, or received as a cash refund—that ITC amount must be deducted from the Section 37 pool in the subsequent taxation year pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(e). If reductions to the Section 37 pool (such as prior-year ITCs or government assistance) exceed additions and the opening pool balance, the resulting negative balance must be included in the taxpayer’s business income for that year under paragraph 12(1)(v), resetting the opening pool balance for the next year to nil (with the prior-year income inclusion accounted for under paragraph 37(1)(c.1)).
1.3 Enacted 2025/2026 Legislative Reforms (Bill C-15, Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1)

Following public consultations initiated in 2024 and proposals announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025, Parliament enacted comprehensive legislative reforms to the SR&ED program through Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Practitioners must take particular care to distinguish the enacted law in Bill C-15 from earlier transitional announcements: while the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 superseded that proposal and enacted a $6 million expenditure limit. Department of Finance Canada projections in Budget 2025 estimate the net federal fiscal cost of these enhancements at $293 million over five years ($3 million in 2025–2026, $70 million in 2026–2027, $85 million in 2027–2028, $65 million in 2028–2029, and $70 million in 2029–2030).
The enacted Bill C-15 reforms encompass six major structural changes:

items: Doubling of the Enhanced 35% ITC Expenditure Limit to $6 Million: For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024), the maximum annual qualified expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC increased from $3 million to $6 million. Consequently, an eligible corporation can now generate up to $2.1 million in enhanced federal ITCs annually ($6,000,000 × 35%), double the previous maximum of $1.05 million.

Expansion of the Taxable Capital Phase-Out Thresholds ($15 Million to $75 Million): For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada thresholds at which a CCPC's expenditure limit begins to phase out and is completely eliminated were expanded from $10 million and $50 million to $15 million and $75 million, respectively (subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21)).

Extension of the 35% Refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs): For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, access to the enhanced 35% ITC—along with 100% refundability on current expenditures and 40% refundability on capital expenditures up to the $6 million expenditure limit—was extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsections 127(9), 127(10.6), 127(10.61), and 127.1(2.01). An ECPC’s $6 million expenditure limit phases out based on its (or its consolidated group's) average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years between $15 million and $75 million.

Elective Revenue-Based Phase-Out Method for CCPCs: For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs with high taxable capital (for example, capital-intensive clean-tech, biotech, or advanced manufacturing firms with substantial balance-sheet equity or debt) but low commercial revenue may elect under subsection 127(10.31) (stand-alone CCPCs) or subsection 127(10.32) (associated CCPCs) to calculate their $6 million expenditure limit phase-out using the $15 million to $75 million three-year average annual revenue test instead of the prior-year taxable capital test. Where a CCPC is associated with other CCPCs, all CCPCs in the associated group must jointly file the election.

Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures, Equipment Leases, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE): Pre-2014 capital eligibility rules were restored for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) and for equipment lease expenditures that first become payable after December 15, 2024. This includes the re-addition of paragraph 37(1)(b) (pool of deductible SR&ED capital expenditures), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(I), (III), and (VI), paragraph 37(8)(e) (excluding buildings other than prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903), the restoration of First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9), and the consequential repeal of the subsection 37(14) capital look-through rule for property acquired or lease costs incurred on or after December 16, 2024. Under amended subsection 127.1(2.01), the 35% ITC earned on restored capital expenditures within the expenditure limit by a CCPC or ECPC is 40% refundable (yielding a 14% immediate cash refund rate on capital outlays, with the remaining 21% ITC available to offset Part I tax or carry over).

Launch of Optional Pre-Claim Approval (April 1, 2026): As part of the administrative modernization announced alongside Budget 2025, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval program on April 1, 2026, enabling eligible corporations and partnerships with gross business income under $25 million to obtain an official up-front project eligibility determination (valid for up to three years) within eight weeks of submitting Form T1322.

2.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Group Allocation Rules

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit is $6,000,000 (up from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). The expenditure limit is subject to a linear phase-out based on corporate size, measured either by prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (the default method for CCPCs under subsection 127(10.2)) or by three-year average annual revenue (the mandatory method for ECPCs and the elective method for CCPCs; subsection 127(10.6) for ECPCs and subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) for electing CCPCs).
A. Pre-December 16, 2024 Expenditure Limit Formula (CCPCs Only)

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the expenditure limit decreased based on the taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under sections 181.2, 181.3, or 181.4 of the ITA) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for the immediately preceding taxation year. The $3,000,000 expenditure limit began decreasing at $10,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital and reached nil at $50,000,000:
Equivalently, for every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $10,000,000, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit declined by $75,000 (7.5% of the excess taxable capital).
B. Post-December 15, 2024 Expenditure Limit Formula (CCPCs and ECPCs)

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit begins to phase out when the relevant size metric—either prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada for non-electing CCPCs (subsection 127(10.2)) or three-year average annual revenue for ECPCs and electing CCPCs (subsection 127(10.6))—reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated at $75,000,000 (a $60,000,000 phase-out span):

In this formula, M represents either: (1) under the Taxable Capital Method (subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21)), the total taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning of section 181.2, 181.3, or 181.4) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for their immediately preceding taxation year; or (2) under the Revenue Method (subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.61), 127(10.31), and 127(10.32)), the average annual revenue of the ECPC (or consolidated group of ECPCs preparing consolidated financial statements) or the electing CCPC (and its associated CCPCs) over the three preceding fiscal years ending before the current taxation year.

Under this linear formula, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1 for every $10 (10%, or $100,000 per $1,000,000) of prior-year taxable capital or three-year average annual revenue in excess of $15,000,000. For example, a CCPC or ECPC with $45,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital or three-year average revenue ($30,000,000 above the $15,000,000 threshold) has an expenditure limit of $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − $30,000,000) ÷ $60,000,000 = $3,000,000.
C. Group Sharing, Short Taxation Years, and Multiple Taxation Years in a Calendar Year

The expenditure limit operates as a single shared pool across corporate groups. All CCPCs that are associated with one another in a taxation year must share a single expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.21) and allocate it amongst themselves by filing T2 Schedule 49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3). If the associated corporations fail to file an allocation agreement within 30 days after receiving a written request from the Minister, the CRA is empowered under subsection 127(10.4) to allocate the expenditure limit among the group. Similarly, for ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group that prepares consolidated financial statements (presenting assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of group members as a single economic entity), the expenditure limit is calculated using the annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements of the group and must be shared among the consolidated ECPC members under subsections 127(10.61) and 127(10.62), with ministerial allocation authority on failure to file an agreement under subsection 127(10.63).

If a standalone or associated/consolidated corporation has a taxation year of less than 51 weeks (a short taxation year), its expenditure limit (or its allocated share of the group expenditure limit) must be prorated based on the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365:
Prorated Expenditure Limit = Allocated Expenditure Limit × (Number of Days in Taxation Year ÷ 365)

As illustrated in Section 3.1.2 of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if Corporation P is allocated $3,000,000 of a group expenditure limit and has a short taxation year of 184 days (from July 1 to December 31, 2027), its usable expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.5) is $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) = $1,512,328. Similarly, if a CCPC or ECPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated or consolidated with another corporation having a taxation year ending in that calendar year, subsection 127(10.5) applies to prorate and restrict the expenditure limit across those multiple taxation years.
2.3 Carryback, Carryforward, Order of Application, and Loss Restriction Events

When a claimant earns non-refundable ITCs (or chooses not to claim a refund on refundable ITCs where applicable), the credits are first applied under subsection 127(5) to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable in the current taxation year. As established by the Tax Court of Canada in Ainsworth Lumber Co. v. The Queen (98-1052-IT-G, 2001), the permissive statutory wording ("there may be deducted") grants the taxpayer the right to elect the order and extent to which ITCs are deducted.

Any unused SR&ED ITCs remaining after offsetting current-year Part I tax may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in excess of ITCs already claimed in those prior years, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years in the taxpayer's ITC pool under subsection 127(9) to offset future Part I tax payable, after which any unapplied ITC expires.

In contrast to the 20-year expiry of unused ITCs under Section 127, undeducted balances in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures have no carryforward time limit and may be carried forward indefinitely. However, if a corporation or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control of a corporation or a trust gaining a new majority-interest beneficiary), strict streaming rules are triggered. Under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h), when control of a corporation is acquired, its Section 37 pool is reduced to nil at that time, and may only be reinstated and deducted in a subsequent taxation year if the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and strictly to the extent of income from that same business or a similar business (including restored capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) acquired on or after December 16, 2024, per amended clause 37(6.1)(a)(i)(B)). Likewise, under Section 127, an acquisition of control restricts the carryforward of unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control and restricts the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (Allowable vs. Qualified SR&ED Expenditures)
3.1 Election Between the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method

Before computing allowable and qualified SR&ED expenditures on Form T661, a claimant must elect on Line 160 (Proxy Method) or Line 162 (Traditional Method) of Part 1 of Form T661 how it will account for SR&ED overhead and other expenditures for the taxation year. This election is made annually—meaning a claimant can switch between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method from one taxation year to the next—but once Form T661 is filed for a particular taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that year (the election is made under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of subsection 37(8) and, under subsection 37(10), must be filed on the day Form T661 is first filed for the year).

body.text: 3.2 Mechanics of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and the Overall Proxy Cap

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)), it foregoes claiming actual overhead and other expenditures in its Section 37 deduction pool, instead deducting those actual utility, facility, clerical, and supply costs as ordinary business deductions. For the purpose of calculating qualified expenditures to earn an ITC under subsection 127(9), the claimant adds the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 502 of Form T661. Because the PPA is a purely notional statutory amount, it is never added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures.

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA has been fixed at 55% of the claimant's SR&ED salary base since the 2014 taxation year (following a phased reduction from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013). Computing the PPA in Part 5 of Form T661 requires a three-step statutory filtration:

items: Determination of the Salary Base and Mandatory Exclusions (Regulations 2900(4), 2900(5), and 2900(9)): The salary base consists solely of the portion of salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (plus permissible salaries for work outside Canada under subsection 37(1.4)). Under the All or Substantially All (ASA) rule in Regulation 2900(5), if an employee spends 90% or more of their working time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is included. However, pursuant to Regulation 2900(9), for all employees (both regular and specified employees), the salary base must exclude taxable benefits under Section 6, stock option benefits under Section 7, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, deemed-paid vacation/holiday/deferred amounts, prior-year unpaid salaries or wages paid in the current taxation year (Line 310 of Form T661), and employment inducement or non-competition payments.

Specified Employee Salary Base Restrictions (Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8)): For any "specified employee"—defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a "specified shareholder" (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, including shares owned by non-arm's-length persons) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, or relative of a controlling shareholder)—Regulation 2900(7) caps the amount that can be included in the PPA salary base (reported in Part 5, Section A, Boxes 852–860 of Form T661) at the lesser of three amounts: (a) the actual eligible salary or wages of the specified employee directly engaged in SR&ED (Box 856 = Box 852 total base salary × Box 854 SR&ED %); (b) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED) for the year, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year; or (c) 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) (established under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan) for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was employed by the claimant in the taxation year (Box 858): Maximum YMPE Salary Base Cap = 2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365) where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days in the year before the individual became a specified employee). Under Regulation 2900(8), if a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the aggregate amount included in the salary bases across all associated corporations cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE.

The Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(6)): Once the preliminary PPA is computed as 55% of the total restricted salary base (Line 820 of Part 5, Section B), Regulation 2900(6) imposes an overall cap to ensure that the notional PPA, combined with claimed SR&ED deductions and specific statutory write-offs, does not exceed the claimant's total business expenses deducted for tax purposes in the year. The overall PPA cap is determined by the statutory formula: Overall PPA Cap = A − B − C In this formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing the claimant's net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold); B is the sum of all deductions claimed in computing business income for the year under specific provisions of the ITA listed in Regulation 2900(6)—namely Section 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, and bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents or brokers), Section 37 (SR&ED expenditure deductions), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and Section 104 (trusts); and C is the total amount of expenditures incurred in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building (such as facility rent). If the claimant carries on more than one business, the specified amounts deducted across all businesses are aggregated. The final allowable PPA carried to Line 502 of Form T661 is the lesser of 55% of the salary base and the Overall PPA Cap (A − B − C).

body.text: 3.3 Salaries and Wages (SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy)

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under Subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (Sections 5 to 8). Consequently, dividends paid to shareholder-employees, drawings by sole proprietors or partners, retiring allowances (excluded by definition from salary or wages), and stock option benefits (Section 7 / Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149, disallowed for taxation years after November 14, 2005) do not constitute SR&ED salary or wages. Taxable benefits (such as automobile benefits, housing/board/meals, group term life insurance, or employer savings plan matches) may be included in SR&ED salary or wages if they involve a cash outlay or represent a reasonable estimate of actual costs incurred by the employer (excluding GST/HST or PST unless no input tax credit is claimable, and provided the underlying cost is not also deducted as a regular business expense), though all taxable benefits are excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9).
A. Directly Engaged vs. Traditional Method Wages and Eligible Tasks

Whether an employee's remuneration qualifies as SR&ED salary or wages depends on the tasks actually performed rather than the employee's job title (SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy). Hands-on experimentation, testing, prototype construction, engineering design, mathematical modelling, and direct technical supervision of ongoing experiments constitute "directly engaged" tasks under both the Proxy Method (Section 7.0 of the policy) and the Traditional Method (Section 8.0). This includes technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year (such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, and specifying material qualities) as well as tasks performed by non-specialized employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine), provided those non-specialized employees are supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications.

Under the Traditional Method, a claimant may also claim on Line 360 (as SR&ED overhead and other expenditures): (1) the employer's share of related payroll benefits (such as CPP, EI, and group benefit contributions) for SR&ED employees, and (2) the salary or wages of clerical and administrative staff (e.g., human resources, accounting, or purchasing personnel) to the extent that their non-technological services directly aid ongoing SR&ED claimed in the year and are incremental (Section 9.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and Section 4.1 of the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy). Under the Proxy Method, all employer-paid related benefits and administrative/clerical wages are excluded from Form T661 and covered by the 55% PPA.
B. Specified Employee Remuneration Limits and Form T1174

In addition to the PPA salary base restrictions under Regulation 2900(7) discussed in Section 3.2, specified employees are subject to specific statutory rules under subsections 37(9) to 37(9.5) of the ITA that apply regardless of whether the claimant uses the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method. First, under subsection 37(9), no amount of a bonus or remuneration based on profits paid or payable to a specified employee may be included in SR&ED salary or wages. By contrast, bonuses and profit-based remuneration paid to non-specified regular employees are allowable as SR&ED salary or wages for the Section 37 pool and ITC calculation, though excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9). Under an administrative position in the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, if an employee's only remuneration in the year for performing SR&ED duties was structured as a bonus or profit-based payment, an amount commensurate with the performance of those SR&ED duties will be accepted as salary or wages for both the Section 37 pool and the PPA calculation, provided all necessary payroll withholdings and procedures were followed. Second, subsections 37(9.1) to 37(9.5) limit the allowable SR&ED salary or wages for specified employees and require associated corporations to allocate the specified employee salary limit among the group by filing Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).

body.text: C. Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5))

As a general rule, expenditures for SR&ED carried on physically outside Canada cannot be included in the subsection 37(1) pool or earn an ITC under Section 127, although current foreign R&D expenses are deductible against business income under subsection 37(2), and work in Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone is covered under subsection 37(1.3). However, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) provide a specific statutory exception for "permissible salary or wages" paid to employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada.

Under Section 10.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), salary or wages for SR&ED work outside Canada are deemed to be incurred in Canada (and thus qualify for the Section 37(1) pool, the PPA salary base, and the Section 127 ITC) if all five statutory conditions are satisfied:

items: The SR&ED work outside Canada was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (payments to contractors performing work outside Canada never qualify under subsection 37(1.4));
The employee was a resident of Canada at the time the salary or wage expense was incurred;
The work related to a business of the claimant;
The work outside Canada was solely in support of, and formed an integral part of, core SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant; and
The claimant reasonably believes that the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by another country because of the employee's presence or activity in that country.

body.text: Under subsection 37(1.5), the maximum permissible salary or wages for work outside Canada that may be claimed in a taxation year is the lesser of Amount A (total actual eligible salary or wages for SR&ED outside Canada meeting the criteria above) and Amount B, which is 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages incurred for SR&ED carried on inside Canada across all projects in the taxation year (Line 306 of Form T661, plus directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting wages claimed on Line 360 under the Traditional Method, but excluding clerical or administrative wages on Line 360). On Form T661, permissible outside-Canada wages are reported on Line 307 (for regular employees) and Line 309 (for specified employees), subject to the strict form constraint that Line 307 plus Line 309 cannot exceed 10% of Line 306, meaning Line 309 cannot exceed (10% × Line 306) minus Line 307.
D. The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4))

Pursuant to subsection 78(4) of the ITA, if any salary, wages, or other remuneration accrued in a taxation year remains unpaid on the 180th day following the end of that taxation year, the expenditure is deemed not to have been incurred in the taxation year for both Section 37 deduction purposes and Section 127 ITC purposes. Instead, the unpaid remuneration is deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. A payment made on the 180th day itself satisfies the deadline, and reasonable accrued vacation or holiday pay and deferred amounts under a salary deferral arrangement are treated as deemed paid on the 180th day. Unpaid remuneration must be identified on Line 315 of Form T661 in the taxation year it was accrued, and when subsequently paid in a later year, it is claimed on Line 310 of Form T661 (though excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9)).
3.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Production Runs, Asset Development, and ITC Recapture

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I), (A)(II), and (B)(V) of the ITA, and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, a claimant may include in both its Section 37 pool and its Section 127 qualified expenditures the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.
A. The "Body of a Thing" Requirement and Timing (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

The CRA’s Materials for SR&ED Policy establishes a strict physical test: to constitute "materials for SR&ED", the raw materials, substances, or component items must be physical and tangible (existing in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) and must compose the "body of a thing" at a given moment in the SR&ED process—meaning they physically form part of a tangible object on which the SR&ED is being conducted or a tangible object resulting from the SR&ED. Materials Consumed (Line 320) are raw materials, substances, or items that are destroyed, absorbed, used up, or rendered virtually valueless as a direct result of the SR&ED experimentation or testing (e.g., chemicals, growth media, seeds, fertilizers, printing ink, or cardboard boxes destroyed during process testing). Materials Transformed (Line 325) are materials or purchased component parts that are incorporated into another physical object, prototype, custom product, or commercial asset that retains value after the SR&ED work concludes.

The cost of materials—which may be purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers and include preparatory service costs such as third-party galvanization required prior to testing—can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in SR&ED, never in an earlier year when they are merely purchased or placed into inventory. Items that do not compose the "body of a thing"—such as laboratory glassware (petri dishes, beakers, pipettes, flasks), cleaning supplies, lubricants, CDs/DVDs, software licences, or general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas)—are excluded from materials for SR&ED, though lab supplies and incremental utilities may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead under the Traditional Method. Furthermore, where materials are purchased from a non-arm's-length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) strips any non-arm's-length profit margin from the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes.
B. Experimental Development in Manufacturing: Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP) and Developing an Asset

When experimental development takes place within an industrial manufacturing facility or involves constructing physical assets, two specialized CRA policies govern cost eligibility. Under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, industrial trial runs are divided into two contexts. Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP) applies only when there is a demonstrable technical risk to the process or product directly attributable to technological uncertainties—such as operating outside known parameter tolerances where process instability, equipment damage, or out-of-spec output is a genuine risk, corroborated by senior management risk authorization, dedicated experimental operating instructions, and analyzed test data. In an ED+EP run, the full labour and materials consumed or transformed for the required experimental production volume are allowable; however, any output beyond what is strictly necessary to validate the hypothesis constitutes "excess production", and all labour, overhead, and material costs for excess production are disallowed. Conversely, Experimental Development with Commercial Production (ED+CP) applies whenever experimental development occurs concurrently with ongoing commercial production without meeting the ED+EP technical risk standard. In an ED+CP run, standard commercial production wages and standard raw materials are strictly disallowed; only incremental (additional) costs—such as specialized SR&ED engineering time and incremental material waste or scrap above normal commercial processing loss—are allowable. Where isolating SR&ED costs in an ED+CP run is impossible and the CRA agrees, an incremental cost method (Actual ED+CP Run Costs minus Standard Commercial Production Costs) may be used.

Similarly, the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy categorizes physical assets into four classes: Prototypes, Pilot Plants, Commercial Plants, and Custom Products / Commercial Assets. A prototype is an original trial model built solely to test a hypothesis and having no lasting value; 100% of its design, construction, and testing labour and consumed or transformed materials qualify as current SR&ED expenditures. A pilot plant is a non-commercial scale facility isolated from normal business operations and dedicated during its useful life to investigating processing steps; provided it is never intended for conversion to commercial operations, labour and materials to resolve uncertainties in developing and operating the pilot plant qualify. Conversely, where a commercial plant or custom product / commercial asset is built for commercial operation or sale, any engineering, construction, or materials that would have been incurred had the technology already existed are excluded; only the labour and consumed or transformed materials directly required to overcome the specific technological uncertainties qualify. Where segregating SR&ED costs from commercial construction of a custom product is impossible, the CRA and the claimant may agree to the Alternative Approach (estimating incremental costs above baseline commercial construction costs plus transformed materials), conditional on the claimant signing a waiver of objection and appeal rights under subsection 169(2.2) of the ITA.
C. Investment Tax Credit Recapture (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

To prevent taxpayers from retaining SR&ED tax credits on physical assets or transformed materials that are subsequently monetized in commerce, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA impose ITC Recapture (Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy). If a taxpayer disposes of a property (sells it) or converts it to commercial use after earning an SR&ED ITC on that property (including materials transformed into a custom product, experimental production, or commercial asset, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, animals or growing things, or physical property acquired under an arm's-length SR&ED contract), the taxpayer must add back the recaptured ITC to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion.

Crucially, as illustrated in Section 7.1.1 of the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant manufactures a prototype or component in-house, ITC recapture applies only to the cost of the materials transformed (Line 325), and never to the in-house SR&ED salaries, wages, or overhead incurred to manufacture the item (Section 6.1). Conversely, if the claimant pays an arm's-length supplier $12,000 to develop and manufacture a component under an SR&ED contract, the entire $12,000 contract property cost is subject to ITC recapture upon sale or commercial conversion under subsections 127(27) and 127(32). Contracts generating purely intellectual property (IP) without physical property acquisition are not subject to ITC recapture when the IP is sold or converted to commercial use. Whenever an ITC is recaptured under subsection 127(27), the recaptured dollar amount is added back to the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).

The Income Tax Act draws a sharp legal distinction between SR&ED Contracts (performed on behalf of the claimant) and Third-Party Payments (funding independent research at approved institutions or corporations), as well as between arm's-length and non-arm's-length (NAL) performers.

body.text: Since January 1, 2013, only 80% of arm's-length contract expenditures and third-party payments enter the qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes under subparagraph 127(9)(a)(ii). Furthermore, for an arm's-length contract expenditure to qualify for the 80% ITC inclusion, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" (subsection 127(9)). If a contract payment is made to a non-taxable supplier, the payer earns 0% ITC. Where a contract is performed partially inside Canada and partially outside Canada, the contract expenditure must be reasonably allocated (e.g., based on fair market value): the Canadian portion is allowable on Form T661 (80% qualified for ITC), while the foreign portion is excluded from Form T661 and earns no ITC, though it may be deducted under subsection 37(2).

When a claimant subcontracts purely support work (paragraph 248(1)(d), such as standalone testing, machining, or computer programming) to an arm's-length contractor that is commensurately supporting the claimant's own Canadian SR&ED, the claimant can claim the contract expenditure (at 80% for ITC), whereas the arm's-length performer cannot claim SR&ED tax credits on standalone support work. Conversely, if a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer is contracted solely to perform support work for a related claimant's Canadian SR&ED, paragraph 248(1)(d) permits the NAL performer to claim those support expenditures as SR&ED, and the NAL performer may transfer the resulting qualified expenditures (including its 55% PPA) to the payer up to the contract amount by filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13). Moreover, while between 2014 and December 15, 2024, subsection 37(14) required a payer to look through an SR&ED contract or third-party payment and reduce its claim by any capital or lease expenditure incurred by the performer (with performer reporting under subsection 37(15)), subsection 37(14) is repealed for property acquired and lease costs incurred on or after December 16, 2024.

Finally, for current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as arm's-length contractor invoices, material purchases, overhead, or third-party payments), if an accrued expenditure remains unpaid on the 180th day after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred, subsection 127(26) deems the expenditure not to have been incurred in that year for Section 127 ITC purposes only, whereas it remains deductible in the Section 37 pool in the year incurred. As illustrated in the Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, if a claimant incurs a $100,000 arm's-length SR&ED contract in Year 1 that remains unpaid 180 days after year-end, $20,000 is deducted as the standard 20% contract reduction and the remaining $80,000 is deducted on Line 520 of Form T661 in Year 1. When the $100,000 invoice is paid in Year 2, $80,000 (80% of the paid contract) is added back on Line 500 of Form T661 in Year 2. Crucially, if an unpaid expenditure is not identified on Form T661 within the 18-month reporting deadline for the taxation year in which it was originally incurred, it will never be included in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes when paid in a future year.
3.6 Overhead, Cloud Computing, and Software Licences (SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy)

When a claimant elects the Traditional Method, it may claim on Line 360 of Form T661 expenditures of a current nature that are "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA and Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3). To satisfy the statutory "directly attributable" standard under Regulation 2900(2)(c), an expenditure (or a reasonably allocated portion thereof) must pass a strict two-pronged test:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: There must be an immediate, direct connection—without any intervening step or intermediary—between the expenditure and at least one of three elements: (a) the SR&ED work itself, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform the SR&ED.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure (or allocated portion) would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred ("but for" the SR&ED work).

body.text: For software, artificial intelligence (AI), and SaaS companies, cloud hosting costs (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud Platform) must be strictly segregated in accounting records using resource tags between production infrastructure (live customer hosting, which is Cost of Goods Sold and ineligible for SR&ED) and development, staging, or R&D infrastructure. Under the Traditional Method, variable R&D cloud computing costs and current software or software licence expenditures that are directly related to the SR&ED work and incremental qualify on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures. Under the Proxy Method, Line 360 cannot be claimed; overhead expenses are covered by the 55% PPA, though computer hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are excluded from the definition of General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) and may qualify under the restored post-December 15, 2024 capital or equipment lease provisions where statutory criteria are met.

Similarly, under the SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, fixed monthly payments for internet, telephone, or cellular plans are ordinary business expenses that are non-incremental and do not qualify regardless of employee usage, whereas specific, identifiable, directly related, and incremental charges (such as long-distance telephone charges or metered electricity usage where power consumption varies directly with SR&ED equipment operation) qualify on Line 360 under the Traditional Method. With respect to personnel recruitment and severance, headhunter fees, job advertising, interview travel, and work permit or immigration costs incurred to hire SR&ED personnel are ineligible (deductible only as regular business expenses), whereas moving expenses related to relocating selected candidates or transferring SR&ED employees to another facility within Canada (subsection 62(3)), as well as a proportional allocation of a retiring allowance paid to a hands-on SR&ED employee based on their career SR&ED salary ratio (Section 4.4), qualify on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental.
3.7 Restored Capital Expenditures, Equipment Lease Costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

From January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, expenditures of a capital nature and equipment lease costs were excluded from the federal SR&ED program. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, capital property, equipment leases, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) are once again eligible for SR&ED tax incentives, subject to strict transition dates and usage thresholds.
A. SR&ED Capital Expenditures (SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, Updated June 29, 2026)

Under restored paragraph 37(1)(b), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III), and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a claimant may claim on Line 390 (and detail the 20 most expensive items in Part 6B, Boxes 780, 782, and 786 of Form T661) expenditures made to acquire depreciable property if all of the following conditions are met:

items: Acquisition and Available-for-Use Window: The depreciable property must be acquired after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) and become available for use (subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024.
Ownership Interest: The expenditure must result in the claimant owning (or obtaining a depreciable leasehold interest in) the property (subsection 13(21) and paragraph 20(1)(a)).

The All or Substantially All (ASA, ≥90%) Intent Test: At the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend either: (a) that the property will be used during all or substantially all (ASA, defined by the CRA as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada (Operating Time Test), or (b) that ASA (90% or more) of the property's value will be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (Value Test).

Full Acquisition Cost & CCA Interaction: Capital cost (Box 782) includes the purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other direct acquisition outlays. When an SR&ED capital expenditure is deducted under Section 37, subsection 37(6) deems the deduction to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA); accordingly, capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance).

body.text: Several statutory exclusions apply to capital expenditures. First, non-depreciable assets such as land, inventory, and goodwill never qualify. Second, under paragraph 37(8)(e), buildings and leasehold interests in buildings are statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures, with the narrow exception of a prescribed special-purpose building approved on a building-by-building basis under Section 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations. Third, under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, bookshelves, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, and calculators) is excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures, whereas under the Traditional Method, GPOEF used ≥90% for SR&ED can be claimed. Crucially, computers—including hardware, software, and ancillary equipment—are not considered GPOEF and therefore qualify under both the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method. Fourth, expenditures to acquire or refurbish used depreciable property meeting the 90% ASA test after December 15, 2024, are reported on Line 390 (and subtracted on Line 535) so that they enter the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, but are prescribed under paragraph 2902(b) of the Regulations to be excluded from qualified expenditures, meaning used equipment earns 0% ITC.
B. Equipment Lease Expenditures (SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, Updated June 8, 2026)

Lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada are claimable as current expenditures, reported per project in Part 6A of Form T661 (whose column total must equal the sum of Lines 350 and 355 in Part 3). Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment (including GPOEF) is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time in the taxation year for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350. If leased equipment (including GPOEF) is used less than 90% of its operating time for SR&ED (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c)), the proportional SR&ED usage percentage of the lease cost is claimed on Line 360 as an overhead and other expenditure, provided it is directly related and incremental. Lease of land is also allowable on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly attributable, whereas building rent is excluded (paragraph 37(8)(e)).

Under the Proxy Method, GPOEF leases, land leases, and building leases are completely excluded. For non-GPOEF leased equipment used ASA (90% or more) of its total operating time in the year for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350. For non-GPOEF leased equipment used primarily (more than 50%, but less than 90%) of its total operating time in the year for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), 50% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 355. For leased equipment used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, 0% can be claimed under the Proxy Method. For any taxation year straddling December 16, 2024, the SR&ED operating time percentage is calculated based on the total operating time of the equipment after December 15, 2024.
C. First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy, Updated May 22, 2026)

When a claimant purchases new depreciable equipment after December 15, 2024, that is used for both SR&ED and commercial production—such that it does not meet the 90% ASA intent test for Line 390 capital expenditures—it may still generate an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) (Line 504 and Part 6C, Boxes 788, 790, and 792 of Form T661). To qualify as SUE, the property must be: (1) depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, (2) new (never previously used, acquired for use, or rented before acquisition), (3) not GPOEF, and (4) not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (which excludes buildings, leasehold interests in buildings, property intended to be used during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing or processing facility or line, or property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes over its expected useful life).
Whether equipment qualifies as SUE depends on its actual use during operating time across two statutory periods:

items: First-Term SUE: The equipment must actually be used primarily (more than 50% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period, which starts when the property is acquired (available for use) and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition. If met, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost of the equipment (excluding borrowed money costs under Section 21, without reference to deemed capital cost rules in subsections 13(7.1) and 13(7.4), and adjusted for non-arm's-length costs under subsection 127(11.6)) is added to qualified expenditures on Line 504 (Box 792) in that first taxation year ending ≥12 months after acquisition.

Second-Term SUE: Provided the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE, if it is actually used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period—which starts at acquisition and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition—an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost is added to qualified expenditures on Line 504 in that second taxation year.

body.text: Unlike Line 390 ASA capital expenditures, the capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the SUE under normal Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any ITC claimed or refunded on SUE reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the following taxation year.
3.8 Government and Non-Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Grant Stacking

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA (Assistance and Contract Payments Policy), the Canadian SR&ED regime is designed to incentivize only the net costs of performing SR&ED in Canada. Consequently, both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 429) and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (Lines 513 to 517) must be reduced dollar-for-dollar by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return for the taxation year.

Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x), government assistance encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or other form of assistance from a federal, provincial, municipal, or foreign government or public authority (including Crown corporations and indirect government funding distributed via non-profit organizations), other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Conditional or forgivable government loans—where repayment depends on future revenues or is capped—are treated by the CRA as government assistance (CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2022). When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED claim, the repayment is added back to the Section 37 pool (paragraph 37(1)(c)) and to qualified expenditures (subsection 127(9)) in the year repaid. Non-government assistance is any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance from a non-governmental entity that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x). Under subsection 127(18), assistance and contract payments reduce qualified expenditures on a project-by-project basis down to nil; excess assistance on one SR&ED project does not spill over to reduce the qualified expenditures of an unrelated SR&ED project (unless allocated among non-arm's-length parties working on the same project using Form T1145 under subsection 127(20)), though assistance exceeding project expenditures is included in income.

When stacking SR&ED with direct federal grants such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC-IRAP) or the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), the grant or conditional contribution reduces the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) and qualified expenditures on Line 515 under subsection 127(18). However, under the Proxy Method, an NRC-IRAP wage grant does not reduce the SR&ED salary base in Part 5 used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Thus, if an employee incurs $100,000 in SR&ED wages and NRC-IRAP reimburses $80,000, the claimant still generates a $55,000 PPA ($100,000 × 55%), resulting in $75,000 of net qualified expenditures ($100,000 wage + $55,000 PPA − $80,000 IRAP grant).

Similarly, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario OITC/ORDTC/OBRITC, Quebec CRIC, or BC SR&ED credit) constitute government assistance for federal tax purposes and reduce both the Section 37 pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures (Line 513/514) in the taxation year in which the expenditures are incurred, unless the claimant formally renounces or waives the provincial credit on or before its income tax return filing-due date (6 months after year-end for corporations). Under Section 4.5 of the Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, when a claimant uses the Proxy Method, the portion of a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional 55% PPA is not deducted from the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) (because the PPA is never in the Section 37 pool); instead, that PPA-related portion of the provincial credit is included in business income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the year received. For Section 127 ITC purposes, however, the entire provincial R&D tax credit (including the portion attributable to the PPA) reduces qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18). Additionally, any provincial "super-allowance benefit amount" (subsection 127(9)) reduces the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d.1) and qualified expenditures under Section 127.
4. Governing Bodies, Pre-Claim Approval, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Penalties
4.1 Governing Institutional Authorities

Administration of Canada’s R&D tax incentive framework is divided between two federal institutions. First, the Department of Finance Canada is responsible for legislative policy design, statutory amendments to the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations, economic impact modelling, and the approval of prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903. Second, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) manages the operational delivery of the SR&ED program across Canada through specialized SR&ED coordinating tax services offices (CTSOs) and tax centres. Within the CRA, claims are evaluated by two distinct specialist cadres: Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) (who report to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM] and evaluate whether the claimed work satisfies subsection 248(1) in an SR&ED Project Eligibility Report) and Financial Reviewers (FRs) (who report to a Financial Review Manager [FRM] and audit expenditure allowability, salary allocations, overhead, contracts, and ITC calculations under Sections 37 and 127). Unlike jurisdictions where a separate science ministry issues binding technical certificates to the tax authority, the CRA retains unified statutory jurisdiction over both the scientific/technological determination and the financial tax assessment.
4.2 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

To provide businesses with up-front certainty before committing R&D capital, the CRA launched the optional Pre-Claim Approval program on April 1, 2026. This formal 2026 program builds upon earlier administrative outreach initiatives, including the 2016 Pre-Claim Consultation (PCC) and Pre-Claim Review (PCR) initiatives, the online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT), and the free SR&ED Service Visit program made permanent on June 20, 2023.

To qualify to apply for Pre-Claim Approval before beginning planned R&D work (or shortly after starting work, before incurring significant costs), the applicant must be a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC), another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership; must have annual gross business income of less than $25 million; and must be in good standing with the CRA. Additionally, the proposed project must not have been included in any previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under litigation.
The Pre-Claim Approval process follows a four-step workflow:

items: Step 1 — Request a Case Number: The business submits a five-minute online web form to confirm basic eligibility. Existing SR&ED claimants in good standing receive a Pre-Claim Approval case number within 2 business days via My Business Account; all other businesses are contacted by phone within 5 business days.

Step 2 — Complete and Upload Form T1322 in My Business Account: Using the assigned case number, the applicant completes and uploads Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval) for up to a maximum of 3 projects (Line 014). Part 1 captures business identification (Lines 010–016), and Part 2, Section A captures project title (Line 020), anticipated project start date (Line 022), estimated total SR&ED expenditures (Line 024), field of science or technology code from Appendix 1 of Guide T4088 (Line 026), and technical contact person (Lines 028–032). In Part 2, Section B, the applicant must answer three technical questions within strict word limits: Line 042 (Maximum 500 words) (What scientific or technological uncertainty do you aim to address?), Line 043 (Maximum 700 words) (What due diligence have you completed to confirm that the scientific or technical uncertainty described in line 042 cannot be resolved using existing knowledge, solutions or approaches?), and Line 044 (Maximum 900 words) (What work do you plan to perform, during the pre-claim approval period (up to 3 years), to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainty described at line 042?). Section C (Lines 050–060) identifies who prepared the responses, Section D requires uploading four supporting document packages (project planning documents, description of planned internal controls for tracking SR&ED time and contemporaneous evidence, key supporting references proving due diligence, and a list of project team members with their credentials), and Part 3 (Lines 080 and 082) requires signed certification.

Step 3 — RTA Evaluation Meeting (Within 4 Weeks): Within four weeks of submitting Form T1322, an assigned CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) conducts a technical evaluation meeting lasting 2 to 5 hours (typically via videoconference with screen-sharing or virtual facility tours). This meeting is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and discretionary for existing claimants in good standing.

Step 4 — Official Determination (Within 8 Weeks) and Accelerated Post-Filing Review (90 Days): Within 8 weeks of receiving the complete application in My Business Account, the CRA issues an official Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report. If granted, the pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years (provided no material uncommunicated changes occur to the project). While the claimant must still file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 after year-end, any refundable SR&ED claim containing only pre-approved projects that is selected for an expenditure review benefits from an accelerated CRA service standard of 90 calendar days—cutting the standard 180-calendar-day review service standard in half. Refundable claims accepted as filed without review have a 60-calendar-day service standard, whereas non-refundable claims have no service standard.

body.text: 4.3 Statutory Filing Deadlines, Prescribed Forms, and Form T661 Architecture

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act (SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, updated January 28, 2025), a taxpayer’s SR&ED reporting deadline is the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. For corporations (T2 Return), because the T2 return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of the taxation year (paragraph 150(1)(a)), the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the corporate taxation year (for example, June 30, 2027, for a December 31, 2025 year-end; note that a tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporation has only 6 months after year-end to file Form T661 and cannot claim an ITC). For individuals / sole proprietorships (T1 Return), the T1 filing-due date is June 15, making their SR&ED reporting deadline June 15 of the following year (12 months after the T1 due date). For trusts (T3 Return), the T3 return is due within 90 days after the trust's taxation year-end, making the SR&ED reporting deadline 15 months (90 days plus 12 months) after the trust's taxation year-end. For partnerships (T5013 Return), Form T661 must be filed by the partnership, and member partners claim their share of ITCs on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) within their respective reporting deadlines.

If a claimant fails to file both prescribed forms (Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) containing all prescribed information on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline (determined by hand-delivery date, postmark date, or Corporation Internet Filing confirmation date, extended to the next business day if the deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday), subsection 37(12) statutorily precludes the expenditures from being treated as SR&ED expenditures, and paragraph 127(9)(m) permanently extinguishes any entitlement to an ITC. Neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada has authority to extend the 18-month deadline (Alex Parallel Computers, Datacalc Research, Easyway Cattle, Westsource, Fooi 2024). A letter expressing an "intent to file" does not satisfy the statutory requirement. The CRA recommends submitting the SR&ED claim together with the tax return, or at least 90 days before the reporting deadline, so the CRA has time to conduct an initial review and advise the claimant of any missing information before the deadline expires.

body.text: On the 2026 version of Form T661, Part 1 captures general claimant details and the annual election between the Proxy Method (Line 160) and Traditional Method (Line 162). Part 2 (Project Information) must be completed for each project claimed (or the 20 largest projects in dollar value at the time of filing) and enforces strict word limits across the three technical narrative boxes: Line 242 (Maximum 350 words) on scientific or technological uncertainties, Line 244 (Maximum 700 words) on the systematic work performed in the taxation year, and Line 246 (Maximum 350 words) on the scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted. Part 2 also captures first-claim vs. continuation indicators (Line 210), capital property names (Line 262), outside-Canada salary indicators (Line 265), and work performed on behalf of another party (Line 266). Part 3 calculates current expenditures on Lines 306 to 370 (excluding current-year unpaid wages on Line 315), summing to Total Current SR&ED Expenditures (Line 380), adds Capital Expenditures (Line 390), and yields Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400). Part 4 calculates the Section 37 deductible pool (Lines 420–470, including assistance reductions on Line 429, recapture of CCA on Line 440, amount available for deduction on Line 455, deduction claimed in the year on Line 460, and carryforward balance on Line 470) and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (Lines 500–570, adding prior-year unpaid non-salary expenses paid in the year on Line 500, the PPA on Line 502, SUE on Line 504, and NAL transfers in on Line 508, and subtracting 20% of arm's-length contracts and third-party payments, provincial/territorial assistance on Lines 513–514, other government assistance on Line 515, non-government assistance and contract payments on Line 517, unpaid current non-salary expenses on Line 520, used capital property on Line 535, and NAL transfers out on Line 540). Part 5 computes the PPA (Boxes 852–858 and Line 820); Part 6A lists leased equipment per project (Line 750); Part 6B lists the 20 most expensive capital expenditures (Boxes 780, 782, 786); Part 6C lists the 20 most expensive SUE items (Boxes 788, 790, 792); Part 9 captures claim preparer disclosures (Lines 935–975); and Part 10 captures officer certification (Lines 165 and 170).
4.4 Statutory Penalties: Claim Preparer Disclosures (s. 162(5.1)) and Gross Negligence (s. 163(2))

The Income Tax Act enforces two distinct penalty regimes specific to SR&ED compliance. First, under subsection 162(5.3), a "claim preparer" is defined as any person or partnership who agrees to accept consideration (a fee) to prepare, or assist in the preparation of, an SR&ED form (Form T661), explicitly excluding an employee of the claimant acting in the course of performing their regular duties of employment. In Part 9 of Form T661, the claimant must indicate whether a claim preparer was engaged (Box 1 or Box 2) and, for every paid preparer, report the preparer's name (Line 940), 15-character Business Number (Line 945), billing arrangement code (Line 950, such as Code 1 for contingency fee, Code 2 for hourly rate, or Code 4 for flat fee), billing rate (Line 955), other billing arrangements (Line 960, maximum 10 words), and total fee paid, payable, or expected to pay (Line 965), followed by certification on Lines 935, 970, and 975. Under the SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, if Part 9 claim preparer information is the only missing, incomplete, or inaccurate prescribed information on Form T661 at the 18-month reporting deadline, the SR&ED claim itself will not be disallowed. However, under subsection 162(5.1), every person or partnership who makes, or participates in, assents to, or acquiesces in the making of, a false statement or omission in respect of claim preparer information required on an SR&ED form is jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable, together with any claim preparer of the form, to a penalty equal to $1,000. Under subsection 162(5.2), a claim preparer is not liable for the $1,000 penalty if they prove due diligence—that they exercised the degree of care, diligence, and skill to prevent the false statement or omission that a reasonably prudent person would have exercised in comparable circumstances.

Second, under subsection 163(2) of the ITA (Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy, updated January 28, 2025), if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (where the CRA bears the burden of showing that the false statement or omission was more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act), makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an original or amended SR&ED claim, the claimant is liable to a penalty equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission (resulting from an understatement of income or a deduction of an overstated ITC against Part I tax payable), plus (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the taxpayer. Under Section 4.3 of the policy, when the gross negligence penalty applies to the refund of a refundable ITC, the CRA calculates the 50% penalty on the entire overstated refund regardless of what caused a portion of the overstatement. Furthermore, in cases of criminal tax fraud or fabricated dates and representations, courts have imposed fines of 150% to 300% of the claimed credits (R v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684; Tempora, SCC 2018) and reopened statute-barred taxation years (Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173).
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory offer dedicated R&D tax credits or innovation grants. All provincial and territorial credits—except those in Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by the Province of Alberta)—are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through the federal T2 and T1 tax system. Three jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—do not offer a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit.
