body.text: 5.1 Quebec’s 2025/2026 CRIC Overhaul (Crédit d’impôt pour la R-D, l’innovation et la précommercialisation)

In its March 25, 2025 Budget Speech (Budget 2025–2026), the Government of Quebec enacted a comprehensive consolidation of its provincial innovation tax regime, introducing the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC). Effective for corporate taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) that begin after March 25, 2025, the CRIC serves as the central pillar of Quebec's innovation tax assistance, delivering $2,412.6 million in gross support over five years (a net increase of $271.5 million after abolishing legacy measures totaling $2,141.1 million).

For corporate taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, the following eight legacy Quebec tax measures are abolished (and can only be claimed for taxation years that began on or before March 25, 2025):

items: Tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V, which previously provided rates ranging from a 14% base rate up to 30% based on corporate assets);
Tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V);
Tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V);
Tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V);
Tax credit for technological adaptation services;
Tax credit for an in-house or external design activity — Industrial Design Component (note that the fashion design component continues to be eligible);
Tax holiday for foreign researchers; and
Tax holiday for foreign experts.

body.text: Unlike the legacy regime—which restricted its 30% enhanced rate based on prior-year corporate assets—the 100% refundable CRIC applies universally to all qualified corporations carrying on business through an establishment in Quebec, regardless of asset size. It provides a 30% enhanced rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures in excess of the corporation's annual exclusion threshold (where the $1,000,000 limit is shared among associated corporations using Form RD-1029.8.EN-T), and a 20% base rate on all eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 limit.

For each taxation year or fiscal period, a claimant must subtract an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold, calculated by multiplying the basic personal amount under the Quebec personal income tax system for each eligible employee by the proportion of that employee's working time spent carrying out eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities. As illustrated in a practitioner calculation for 2025 using a basic personal amount of $18,751, a corporation with 10 full-time R&D employees has an exclusion threshold of 10 × $18,751 = $187,510.

In addition to Quebec R&D activities, the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities—defined as tests, technological validations, studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements, and product design, provided those activities constitute a continuation of R&D activities carried out in Quebec by or on behalf of the corporation or partnership. Eligible expenditures include salaries and wages, subcontractor payments (including 50% of subcontracts entered into with a university, public research centre, or research consortium), payments to research organizations, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of property. Furthermore, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Quebec nexus ratio for the Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI) is calculated using R&D expenditures giving entitlement to the CRIC (without reduction by the CRIC exclusion threshold, and excluding pre-commercialization expenditures). To claim the CRIC with Revenu Québec, corporations file Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting SR&ED Expenditures), Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)), Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (associated group $1M limit agreement), and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (pre-commercialization component).
5.2 Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Other Provincial Regimes

In Ontario (Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), Sections 38–45 and 97), corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment can access three distinct credits. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, Schedule 566) provides an 8% refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum $240,000 credit for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016). Ontario updated the OITC so that qualified expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (whereas capital expenditures between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, were excluded, and pre-2014 capital expenditures were included at 40%). The $3 million OITC expenditure limit phases out if prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or if prior-year taxable paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC, Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit with no expenditure limit (3-year carryback, 20-year carryforward; written waiver permitted within 6 months of year-end). Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC, Schedules 568 and 569, Schedule 5 Line 470) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified monetary contract payments (not payments-in-kind, capped at $20,000,000 annually across an associated group for a maximum $4,000,000 refundable credit) paid to an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) in Ontario (universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence), provided the corporation is not connected to the ERI (>10% voting rights or fair market value of shares or non-arm's-length relationship).

In British Columbia (Income Tax Act (BC), Sections 97–103; Form T666), BC Budget 2026 made the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent. Moreover, British Columbia harmonized with the federal Bill C-15 reforms for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024: (1) the 10% refundable BC credit is extended to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) in addition to CCPCs; (2) the annual expenditure limit for the 10% refundable credit doubled from $3 million to $6 million (yielding up to $600,000 in refundable BC credits), phasing out between $15 million and $75 million of prior-year taxable capital; and (3) capital expenditures restored federally on or after December 16, 2024, qualify as BC qualified expenditures. Non-refundable BC credits (for expenditures above the limit or by non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporations, including active corporate partners of partnerships) may be carried back 3 years or forward 10 years (or renounced), and BC recapture applies if SR&ED property is sold or converted to commercial use within 10 years. Form T666 must be filed within 18 months of the taxation year-end.

In Alberta (Alberta Corporate Tax Act, Sections 26.95–26.99; AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970), the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a refundable payment on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta R&D expenditures matching federal SR&ED rules, calculated as an 8% payment on eligible spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (its average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two years), and an enhanced 20% payment on eligible spending exceeding that two-year base level. In Saskatchewan (The Income Tax Act, 2000 (SK), Sections 63–63.4; Schedule 403), the province provides a 10% tax credit. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Saskatchewan increased the annual qualifying expenditure limit for the 10% refundable credit for CCPCs from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 (up to $200,000 refundable, reported on Schedule 5 Line 645), while expenditures above $2,000,000 (and all expenditures by non-CCPCs) earn a 10% non-refundable credit (Schedule 5 Line 631, 3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward) up to a combined refundable and non-refundable maximum annual credit cap of $1,000,000 ($10,000,000 in eligible expenditures).

In Manitoba (Section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba), Schedule 380), corporations earn a 15% R&D tax credit (half refundable [7.5%] and half non-refundable [7.5%] for in-house R&D, and 100% refundable [15%] for R&D under contract with a qualifying institute in Manitoba, with contract payments to eligible Manitoba educational institutions 100% eligible rather than reduced to 80%). In Atlantic Canada and the North, Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301 / Form T1129, where eligible expenditures are uniquely not reduced by government or non-government assistance other than GST/HST input tax credits), and Yukon (Schedule 442 / Form T1232, offering 15% plus an additional 5% on payments to Yukon University) all provide 15% fully refundable R&D tax credits.
5.3 Integrated Federal-Provincial Calculation Methodology (Worked Numerical Example)

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of the Proxy Method, the post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditure rules, and provincial credit assistance reduction (paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18)), consider an Ontario CCPC (a qualifying corporation with $5 million in prior-year taxable capital and $300,000 in prior-year taxable income, qualifying for the full $6M federal expenditure limit and full $3M Ontario OITC limit) during its taxation year ending December 31, 2026:

items: Incurred SR&ED Costs in Ontario (2026): The corporation incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries of regular (non-specified) employees in Ontario (Line 306), $100,000 in materials consumed (Line 320), $200,000 in arm's-length Canadian SR&ED subcontractor invoices paid within 180 days (Line 340), and $300,000 for new specialized R&D testing equipment acquired and available for use in March 2026 intended for ≥90% (ASA) SR&ED use (Line 390 capital expenditure).

Form T661 Part 3 (Allowable SR&ED Expenditures): Total Current SR&ED Expenditures (Line 380) equal $1,000,000 + $100,000 + $200,000 = $1,300,000, and Total Capital SR&ED Expenditures (Line 390) equal $300,000, yielding Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400) of $1,600,000.

Form T661 Part 5 (Prescribed Proxy Amount at 55%): On the $1,000,000 SR&ED salary base, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 820 / Line 502, assuming the overall A − B − C cap is not binding) is 55% × $1,000,000 = $550,000.

Gross Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Before Provincial Assistance): Current qualified expenditures equal $1,000,000 (wages) + $100,000 (materials) + $160,000 (80% × $200,000 contract) + $550,000 (PPA) = $1,810,000, and capital qualified expenditures equal $300,000 (100% eligible post-December 15, 2024), summing to $2,110,000 in gross qualified expenditures.

Provincial Credits (Ontario OITC at 8%; Assuming Waiver of Non-Refundable ORDTC): Under Schedule 566, the 8% refundable Ontario OITC applies to the full $2,110,000 of qualified expenditures (including 100% of post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures), yielding $168,800 in refundable OITC ($144,800 on current qualified expenditures—including $44,000 attributable to the $550,000 PPA—and $24,000 on the $300,000 capital expenditure).

Net Federal Section 37 Pool and Net Federal Section 127 Qualified Expenditures: For the Section 37 Deductible Pool (Line 455), Total Allowable Expenditures ($1,600,000) are reduced only by the portion of the OITC not attributable to the PPA ($168,800 − $44,000 = $124,800, per Section 4.5 of the Assistance Policy, while the $44,000 PPA portion is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) when received), leaving a Section 37 deductible pool of $1,475,200. For Net Federal Qualified Expenditures (Line 570), Total Gross Qualified Expenditures ($2,110,000) are reduced by the entire $168,800 OITC (Line 513/514), leaving $1,941,200 (comprising $1,665,200 net current qualified expenditures and $276,000 net capital qualified expenditures).

Federal Investment Tax Credit (35% Rate) and Cash Refundability (Section 127.1(2.01)): The 35% federal ITC on net current qualified expenditures is 35% × $1,665,200 = $582,820 (100% refundable in cash = $582,820), and the 35% federal ITC on net capital qualified expenditures is 35% × $276,000 = $96,600 (40% refundable in cash = $38,640, with the remaining $57,960 ITC available to offset Part I tax or carry back 3 / forward 20 years). In total, the corporation earns $848,220 in combined federal and Ontario OITC tax credits (53.01% of its $1,600,000 cash outlay), of which $790,260 ($582,820 + $38,640 + $168,800) is refunded immediately in cash.

body.text: 6. Jurisprudence, Case Law Precedents, and CRA Audit Defence Architecture
6.1 The Foundational Five-Criteria Test (Northwest Hydraulic) and the 2021 CRA Guidelines

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is the landmark decision of Chief Justice Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC). In Northwest Hydraulic, the Court established the five-part common-law framework for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Routine engineering describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Crucially, Northwest Hydraulic established the doctrine of "system uncertainty": a technological uncertainty may exist even where all individual components or sub-processes are physically known or off-the-shelf, if there is genuine scientific or technological uncertainty regarding how those components will interact when integrated into a complex system.

Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This requires a five-stage intellectual discipline: (a) observing the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulating a clear objective; (c) identifying and articulating the technological uncertainty; (d) formulating a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodically and systematically testing the hypotheses.

Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? The investigation must be characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, rather than intuitive, unrecorded trial-and-error, evaluated flexibly in the context of applied sciences and the taxpayer's business environment.

Did the process result in a technological advancement? A technological advancement is an advancement in the general understanding of scientific or technological relations—including negative knowledge (proving through systematic testing that a hypothesis does not work, as affirmed in Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 1081)—rather than mere commercial novelty or a feature that is only new to the claimant.

Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed? Contemporaneous documentation generated naturally as the investigation unfolds provides the primary evidentiary foundation for proving that a systematic investigation occurred.

body.text: On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived its former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and replaced it with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The 2021 Guidelines consolidate the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria into two overarching requirements. First, the "Why" Requirement mandates that work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement (paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(c)), which arises when there is a scientific or technological uncertainty due to an insufficiency in reasonably available scientific or technological knowledge, seeking conceptual knowledge (theories or predictive models) rather than merely factual knowledge. Second, the "How" Requirement mandates that work be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, comprising four mandatory elements: (1) generating a hypothesis consistent with known facts; (2) testing the hypothesis by experiment or analysis; (3) developing logical conclusions based on the experimental results; and (4) keeping evidence generated as the work progresses.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88), decided on May 10, 2021, the taxpayer argued that the scientific-method criterion should not apply because the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) does not mention the scientific method; the Federal Court of Appeal rejected that argument, noting that it had repeatedly endorsed the Northwest Hydraulic approach. In National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72, affirming 2020 TCC 47), the taxpayer argued that the CRA’s 2021 Guidelines relaxed the common-law test or eliminated the requirement to follow the scientific method. The Federal Court of Appeal rejected that argument, holding that CRA administrative commentary is not legally binding on the courts, that the "Why" and "How" framework still requires underlying scientific rigour and discipline, and that the five-criteria test from Northwest Hydraulic remains the binding legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act.
6.2 Catalog of Landmark and Modern Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence (1988–2026)

headers: Judicial Holding and Practical Audit Takeaway

cells: Systematic investigation vs. trial-and-error; lack of records.

Held that systematic investigation requires a planned, orderly approach with preserved records of tests and parameters; unrecorded shop-floor trial-and-error where test records are discarded fails the statutory definition.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520
Foundational 5-question test; "system uncertainty" in hydraulic models.
Established the five-criteria common-law test for SR&ED; recognized that integrating known components can create eligible system uncertainty when combined behaviour is unpredictable.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1998] FCJ No. 1890
Documentary "repeatability" burden; inference of systematic research; failed projects.

Reversed the TCC (97 DTC 99); held that requiring documentary proof of exact test "repeatability" is an error of law where credible evidence proves testing occurred and achieved a technological advance. Confirmed that failed research still qualifies for SR&ED.
Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen, 96-4369-IT-G
Definition of technological advancement when hypotheses fail.
Established that the systematic falsification or rejection of a scientific or engineering hypothesis is itself a valid technological advancement.
C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740
Appellate endorsement of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Formally adopted Chief Justice Bowman's five-question framework from Northwest Hydraulic at the Federal Court of Appeal level.
Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, 2007 DTC 41
Burden of proof on technological uncertainty vs. standard practice.
Dismissed the appeal where the taxpayer failed to establish with specific technical evidence how its automated toll gate design met the SR&ED criteria.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355, 2012 DTC 5031
Reaffirmation of the 5-criteria test in product/machinery overhaul.
Confirmed that all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria must be satisfied cumulatively; overhauling existing machinery using known engineering methods is routine development.
Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42, 2017 DTC 1022
Holistic evaluation of integrated engineering systems (pipe-liner mandrel).

Rejected the CRA's attempt to dissect an integrated project into isolated routine tasks; held that coupled material and mechanical constraints must be evaluated holistically and validated ordinary-course photos, test logs, and notes.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88
Judicial role in statutory interpretation of subsection 248(1).

Rejected the argument that the scientific-method criterion does not apply because subsection 248(1) does not mention it; reaffirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, repeatedly endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal, govern the interpretation of SR&ED under subsection 248(1).
National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2020 TCC 47, aff'd 2022 FCA 72
Status of 2021 CRA Guidelines; admissibility and impartiality of expert witnesses.

Held that the 2021 CRA Guidelines did not eliminate the scientific method requirement; upheld exclusion of a taxpayer's expert witness report where the expert acted as an advocate and attempted to introduce unsworn facts.
Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The Queen, 2023 TCC 18
System integration uncertainties in tractor design.
Allowed the appeal where the taxpayer demonstrated complex system integration uncertainties.
Cloud-based SaaS architecture and open-source React/Redux integration.

Landmark software win; held that systemic architectural uncertainties in integrating open-source tools (React/Redux) to overcome performance bottlenecks went beyond routine debugging and satisfied Northwest Hydraulic.
Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173
Plagiarized technical narratives; reopening statute-barred years; s. 163(2) penalties.

Split ruling: allowed genuine 2007–2008 heating element projects, but held that copying supplier/website text into technical narratives constituted misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred years and supported penalties.
Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 183
Reconstructed narratives and arbitrary wage allocations across 13 projects.

Dismissed all 13 projects; held that post hoc reconstructed narratives and splitting employee wages evenly across batches without contemporaneous time records fail both technical and financial substantiation.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7
Software & industrial control: cumulative system uncertainty vs. product scale-up.

Split ruling: allowed the SIL 4 train-control box (MTCLM) project due to cumulative system-level uncertainty unresolvable by available methods, but disallowed $1,293,692 on the SCADACOM-5 upgrade because modernizing and scaling up software with known tools is product development, not experimental development.

body.text: 6.3 CRA Review, Audit Procedures, and Dispute Resolution Architecture

Every SR&ED claim filed with the CRA is processed through the mainframe corporate tax system (CORTAX) and subjected to an automated preliminary risk assessment. Approximately 80% of all SR&ED claims are filed electronically, and roughly 40% of T2 SR&ED claims are accepted as filed at the tax centre stage without audit action based on the automated risk management tool. Claims that are not accepted as filed are routed to a coordinating tax services office through the AIMS case management system for a desktop/virtual or on-site review.

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs), and the Financial Claim Review Manual (FCRM), the review and dispute resolution lifecycle operates under five strict procedural rules:

items: No Right to "Withdraw" a Selected Claim & Unavailability of Voluntary Disclosures: Once an SR&ED claim is selected for review, the claimant cannot withdraw the claim to avoid scrutiny or penalties. Because Form T661 is an integral statutory component of the income tax return and its Part 10 certification attests that the information is true, correct, and complete, any request to withdraw is processed as an amended claim reducing the claim to nil while the CRA audit—and any gross negligence penalty evaluation under subsection 163(2)—continues (RTA Manual, Chapter 3.3.0). Furthermore, the CRA's Voluntary Disclosures Program (VDP) is unavailable once a review has commenced.

Strict Prohibition on Negotiation (Section 5.10.0 of the RTA Manual): CRA Research and Technology Advisors and Financial Reviewers are strictly prohibited from negotiating project eligibility or financial expenditures with claimants (for example, disallowing one project as a trade-off for accepting another project as filed). Every project and expenditure line must be adjudicated solely on its factual and statutory merits.

Requests for Information (Subsection 231.2(1)), Virtual Reviews, and Contemporaneous Evidence: Under subsection 231.2(1) of the ITA (and CRA Communiqués AD-10-01, AD-10-02, and AD-10-03), CRA reviewers have statutory authority to inspect books and records, require assistance on premises, and issue formal Requests for Information (RFIs), granting a standard minimum response window of 30 calendar days (with 15-day extensions for reasonable requests). While most reviews are conducted virtually via videoconference, claimants may request an on-site facility visit on an exceptional basis where virtual presentation hinders collaborative fact-finding. Per Appendix 2 of Guide T4088 and Chapter 10.5.2 of the CRA Audit Manual, contemporaneous documentation—such as source code logs, project progress reports, dated planning documents, test data, scrap records, prototypes, artefacts, and contemporaneous timesheets—carries the highest probative weight (TF98 file).

The Proposal Package and 30-Day Representation Window: If the RTA and FR propose adjustments to eligibility or allowable/qualified expenditures (or propose a penalty), the FR issues a formal Proposal Package containing the RTA's SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and a financial Proposal Letter. The claimant is generally granted 30 calendar days to submit written technical and financial representations rebutting the proposed adjustments.

Three-Step Administrative Dispute Resolution and Formal Notices of Objection (90-Day Statutory Deadline): If a claimant disagrees with review findings, the CRA's three-step administrative dispute resolution process consists of: (a) discussing factual concerns directly with the RTA and FR; (b) escalating unresolved issues to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and Financial Review Manager (FRM); and (c) requesting an Administrative Review (Form RC532) after receiving the Proposal Package. An Administrative Review is not a second technical audit by new reviewers; rather, it verifies whether the review complied with SR&ED legislation, policies, and due process. Once the CRA issues the final Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, a claimant wishing to contest the determination must file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 calendar days from the date on the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, with subsequent statutory appeal rights to the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal.
